summary: Taxable income shapes how Canadian corporations benefit from SR&ED incentives. Under the federal Income Tax Act, qualifying CCPCs receive the 35% investment tax credit as a cash refund on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures regardless of whether they have taxable income, while Ontario's 8% OITC phases out when prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000.

body.text: Taxable income shapes how Canadian corporations benefit from SR&ED incentives. Under the federal Income Tax Act, qualifying CCPCs receive the 35% investment tax credit as a cash refund on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures regardless of whether they have taxable income, while Ontario's 8% OITC phases out when prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000.
Executive Summary and the 2025–2026 Legislative Paradigm Shift

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program serves as the cornerstone of industrial innovation policy in Canada, representing the single largest federal government source of financial support for business-led research and development. Administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada under the authority of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA") and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "ITR"), the program distributed $4.6 billion in investment tax credits (ITCs) across 23,677 processed corporate and unincorporated claims during the 2025–2026 fiscal cycle. Rather than operating as a discretionary competitive grant, the SR&ED regime functions as a statutory entitlement embedded within the federal corporate income tax system, providing claimants with a dual fiscal benefit: an immediate 100% income tax deduction with indefinite carryforward capacity for allowable SR&ED expenditures under section 37 of the ITA, and a separate, potentially refundable Investment Tax Credit ranging from 15% to 35% of qualified expenditures under sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential statutory transformation in over a decade. Following policy proposals first announced in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and refined through draft legislative amendments released by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024—and for capital assets acquired or lease obligations first becoming payable on or after that date—Bill C-15 reversed several restrictive austerity measures that had been imposed by the 2012 Federal Budget and took effect in 2014.

The modernized statutory framework enacted under Bill C-15 implemented six structural reforms across the federal regime that fundamentally alter the after-tax economics of domestic innovation. First, Parliament doubled the maximum annual qualified expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC rate for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, thereby expanding the maximum annual refundable federal cash injection from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Second, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada thresholds governing the phase-out of this enhanced expenditure limit for associated CCPC groups increased from the legacy 10,000,000–50,000,000 bracket to 15,000,000–75,000,000. Third, under new subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), qualifying CCPCs gained the statutory option to elect out of the taxable-capital phase-out in subsection 127(10.2) and instead compute their expenditure limit reduction using average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years within the same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 corridor, preventing balance-sheet-heavy hardware, clean-technology, and life-sciences firms from losing refundable credit access prematurely. Fourth, ending a multi-decade structural penalty against domestic public listings, subsection 127(10.1) and newly enacted subsections 127(10.6) to 127(10.64) extended the enhanced 35% ITC rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), subject to revenue-based phase-out parameters. Fifth, after an eleven-year exclusion period spanning 2014 through 2024, new depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, that is intended for at least 90% SR&ED use over its useful life in Canada—along with eligible equipment lease costs first payable on or after December 16, 2024—once again qualifies for both the section 37 deduction pool under paragraph 37(1)(b) and the section 127 ITC, with enhanced-rate capital ITCs refundable at a 40% rate under amended subsection 127.1(2). Sixth, effective April 1, 2026, the CRA operationalized an optional pre-claim technical approval process utilizing Form T1322 for businesses with gross business income below $25,000,000, granting up to three years of technical project certainty and a 90-day fast-track processing target upon filing.

Concurrently with these federal reforms, provincial tax authorities enacted sweeping structural realignments to harmonize with or recalibrate against the expanded federal base. Most notably, in its 2025–2026 provincial budget, Quebec abolished six legacy R&D tax credit mechanisms—including the long-standing R&D Salaries and Wages tax credit (Form RD-1029.7), the University/Public Research Centre contract credit, and the Research Consortium credit—consolidating them into the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Simultaneously, Quebec restructured its E-Business Tax Credit (CDAE) into the Development of E-Business Tax Credit Integrating Artificial Intelligence (CDAEIA) for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, mandating artificial intelligence integration while gradually shifting credit composition toward non-refundable components through 2028.

body.text: Statutory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
Dual-Pool Mechanics Under Sections 37 and 127 of the Income Tax Act

A foundational principle of Canadian tax auditing is that the calculation of an SR&ED claim requires two interrelated yet legally distinct statutory computations: first, the determination of the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under section 37 of the ITA; and second, the determination of qualified expenditures for Investment Tax Credit purposes under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Treating "allowable SR&ED expenditures" and "qualified expenditures" as interchangeable terms is a critical methodological error in tax working papers because an expenditure may be 100% deductible under section 37 while generating a reduced, modified, or zero ITC under section 127.

Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct in computing income from that business for a taxation year an amount not exceeding the balance in its cumulative SR&ED expenditure pool at the end of the year. Paragraph 37(1)(a) captures expenditures of a current nature—specifically direct salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed, directly related and incremental overhead (under the Traditional Method), arm's-length and non-arm's-length SR&ED contracts performed in Canada, and eligible third-party payments. Following the enactment of Bill C-15, newly restored paragraph 37(1)(b) captures eligible expenditures of a capital nature incurred on depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Because section 37 operates as a cumulative pool, any portion of the pool not deducted in the current taxation year—for instance, when a pre-revenue corporation is in a non-capital loss position or wishes to preserve deductions for future higher-tax years—carries forward indefinitely to subsequent taxation years, subject only to change-of-control streaming restrictions under subsection 37(6.1).

Conversely, section 127 governs the generation and application of Investment Tax Credits against Part I federal income tax otherwise payable. Under subsection 127(9), the definition of qualified expenditure modifies the section 37 pool in three fundamental ways. First, under subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition of qualified expenditure in subsection 127(9), expenditures described in subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) through (iii)—namely arm's-length SR&ED contract payments and third-party payments—are included in qualified expenditures at strictly 80% of the expenditure incurred, reflecting the statutory presumption that 20% of the subcontractor's invoice represents profit markup and non-eligible administrative overhead. Second, payments made to related (non-arm's-length) subcontractors do not qualify as qualified expenditures for the payer under subsection 127(9), even though the underlying cost may be deductible for income tax purposes. Instead, the related party actually performing the SR&ED claims the underlying eligible expenditures, or the parties must utilize statutory expenditure transfer agreements under subsections 127(13) to (20). Third, where a taxpayer elects the Proxy Method on Line 160 of Form T661, the notional overhead amount computed under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR—equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base—is added solely to the section 127 qualified expenditure base for ITC calculation; the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is never added to the section 37 income tax deduction pool.

Furthermore, to prevent double-dipping between the section 37 income deduction and the section 127 tax credit, paragraph 37(1)(e) mandates that any SR&ED ITC claimed (whether used to offset Part I tax or received as a cash refund under section 127.1) in a preceding taxation year must be deducted from the taxpayer's section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year, thereby reducing the pool balance or, if the pool turns negative, triggering an income inclusion under paragraph 12(1)(v).
Bill C-15 and the Modernization of Corporate Eligibility

Historically, Canada's two-tier SR&ED credit structure drew a sharp statutory boundary based on subsection 125(7) of the ITA, which defines a "Canadian-controlled private corporation" (CCPC) as a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation other than a corporation controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (including both de jure voting control and de facto control under subsection 256(5.1)), by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by one or more corporations listed on a designated stock exchange under subsection 256(6.1), or by any combination thereof. Under this historical rule, the moment a domestic technology or life-sciences company completed an initial public offering (IPO) on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) or TSX Venture Exchange (TSXV), or came under technical control of public shareholders, it forfeited its CCPC status and dropped from a 35% fully refundable ITC to a 15% non-refundable ITC.

Bill C-15 directly remedied this distortion for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, by amending subsection 127(10.1) and introducing subsections 127(10.6) through 127(10.64) to create the statutory category of an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC). To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy three cumulative statutory conditions: it must be a resident of Canada and a public corporation (or a corporation that would be a CCPC if its shares were not listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada); its shares must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons; and it must satisfy the consolidated group allocation and reporting requirements under subsections 127(10.61) to 127(10.64) if it is a member of a consolidated public corporate group.
Expenditure Limits, Taxable Capital Phase-Outs, and Revenue Elections

The enhanced 35% ITC rate applies to qualified expenditures up to the claimant's annual expenditure limit for the taxation year. Under subsection 127(10.2), as amended by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the base expenditure limit for a CCPC (or an associated group of CCPCs) increased from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000.

Under the default Taxable Capital Method, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to phase out on a straight-line basis once the taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under Part I.3, sections 181.2 to 181.4 of the ITA) of the CCPC and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000, replacing the pre-December 16, 2024 phase-out thresholds of $10,000,000 and $50,000,000. where TC represents the aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada of the claimant and all associated corporations in the preceding taxation year. Because taxable capital employed in Canada includes share capital, retained earnings, surpluses, and debt obligations (such as loans, advances, bonds, debentures, and notes payable), venture-backed startups and capital-intensive manufacturing or biotechnology enterprises frequently exceeded the legacy $10,000,000 threshold long before generating commercial revenue.

To eliminate this balance-sheet penalty, Bill C-15 introduced an Elective Gross Revenue Method under new subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Where a standalone CCPC or an associated group of CCPCs files this annual election, the taxable-capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) ceases to apply for that taxation year, and the expenditure limit is instead phased out based on the corporation's (or associated group's) average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years, utilizing the identical $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 linear reduction corridor:

where GR is the average annual gross revenue determined over the three preceding fiscal years. For an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC), the expenditure limit is determined under newly enacted subsection 127(10.6) (with former subsection 127(10.6) renumbered as subsection 127(10.5)) using the three-year average gross revenue phase-out mechanism between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000; while the August 2025 draft technical notes initially modelled a $4,500,000 base cap in subsection 127(10.6), the enacted Bill C-15 framework aligns the headline enhanced limit at $6,000,000 across qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs, subject to consolidated group sharing under subsections 127(10.61) to 127(10.64).

When two or more CCPCs are associated with one another in a taxation year (pursuant to section 256 of the ITA), they must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit and file an allocation agreement in prescribed form under subsection 127(10.3) (or under subsections 127(10.62) and 127(10.63) for consolidated ECPCs); failure by the group to file an allocation agreement authorizes the Minister of National Revenue to allocate the limit among the corporations. Furthermore, if a corporation has a short taxation year containing fewer than 365 days—such as upon incorporation, amalgamation, or an acquisition of control—its expenditure limit is prorated strictly by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365. Under renumbered subsection 127(10.5), where a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC that has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year, the expenditure limit for each short taxation year must be prorated by the number of days in that specific short taxation year divided by 365.
Investment Tax Credit Rates, Refundability Matrix, and Carryover Rules

The financial realization of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits depends on the interaction between the rate determination provisions of section 127 and the refundability provisions of section 127.1 of the ITA. Under subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01), refundability varies strictly by corporate classification, expenditure type (current versus capital), and whether the expenditure falls within or above the claimant's annual expenditure limit.

For qualifying CCPCs and non-excluded CCPCs incurring current expenditures within their expenditure limit, subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01) provide a 35% ITC on qualified current expenditures up to the $6,000,000 maximum limit, and 100% of that 35% credit is refundable in cash, yielding up to $2,100,000 in direct cash refund regardless of whether the corporation has taxable income or prior-year profits. Similarly, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) earns the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on qualified current expenditures up to its expenditure limit. With respect to capital expenditures within the expenditure limit for both CCPCs and ECPCs, eligible depreciable property acquired (or lease costs first payable) on or after December 16, 2024, attracts the enhanced 35% ITC rate, but pursuant to amended subsection 127.1(2), the rate of refundability is restricted to 40% of the earned credit, yielding an immediate 14% cash refund on the capital cost with the remaining 21% non-refundable credit available to offset Part I tax. Conversely, qualified expenditures above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, as well as all qualified expenditures incurred by foreign-controlled subsidiaries, non-eligible public corporations, and unincorporated individuals or trusts, earn the basic 15% ITC rate. While a qualifying CCPC under legacy subsection 127.1(2) rules may access 40% refundability on basic 15% current ITCs above its limit if it meets qualifying corporation thresholds, for standard large and foreign-controlled corporations the 15% ITC is strictly non-refundable and only reduces Part I tax payable.

Under subsection 127(5) and the definition of investment tax credit in subsection 127(9), any portion of an earned SR&ED ITC that is not refunded in the taxation year (or used to offset current-year Part I federal tax) may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in those years. Claimants must note that under subsection 127(9), any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash during a taxation year is statutorily deemed to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable for that year, thereby reducing the remaining ITC pool available for carryback or carryforward.
Qualifying Expenditures and Computational Rules
Direct Labour, Specified Employees, and the 10% Foreign Wage Rule

Salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada constitute the primary expenditure base of most claims. Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and subsection 127(9), eligible labour encompasses the portion of base salaries, wages, and taxable benefits paid to engineers, scientists, developers, technicians, and direct first-line technical supervisors proportional to the verified time they spend performing qualifying experimental work or direct technical support work (defined in subsection 248(1) as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research where commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core SR&ED).

Three strict statutory constraints govern the inclusion of salaries and wages in an SR&ED claim. First, under the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule in subsection 78(4) of the ITA, accrued salaries, wages, or bonuses that remain unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred are deemed not to have been incurred in that year and can only be claimed in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid. Second, stringent restrictions apply to specified employees, defined in subsection 248(1) as any employee who is a specified shareholder of the corporation (owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation. For specified employees, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are strictly excluded from SR&ED expenditures, total claimable SR&ED wages are capped at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under the Canada Pension Plan, and for the purpose of calculating the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4), each specified employee's salary base inclusion is further capped at 2.5 times the YMPE (or 75% of total salary and wages before SR&ED allocation, whichever is less).

Third, while SR&ED must generally be carried on physically within Canada (including Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone), subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA (reported on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661) establishes the 10% Permissible Foreign SR&ED Wage Rule. Under subsection 37(1.5), salaries and wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada after February 25, 2008, qualify for the section 37 deduction pool, the section 127 ITC, and the 55% PPA salary base if and only if five cumulative statutory conditions are met: the work must be performed directly by an employee of the claimant (foreign subcontractor labour is 100% excluded); the employee must be a resident of Canada for income tax purposes; the foreign SR&ED activities must be an integral part of, and solely in support of, an SR&ED project carried on in Canada by the claimant (such as field testing at a foreign site or specialized climatic testing unavailable in Canada); the remuneration must not be subject to an income or profits tax imposed by the government of a country other than Canada; and the total claimable foreign SR&ED salary and wages for the taxation year cannot exceed 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salaries and wages incurred for work performed in Canada during that taxation year.
Subcontractor Payments, Non-Arm's-Length Restrictions, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts out SR&ED work to an arm's-length contractor (either an incorporated vendor or an independent unincorporated consultant with a valid Business Number, GST/HST account, or Social Insurance Number), the expenditure is only eligible if the contractor performs the SR&ED work physically in Canada on behalf of the claimant. If a Canadian-registered consulting firm is engaged but sub-delegates or employs software developers or engineers located outside Canada, the claimant must prorate the invoice and may only claim the exact percentage of the contract work physically executed within Canada.

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), 100% of an eligible arm's-length Canadian SR&ED contract expenditure is added to the section 37 deductible expenditure pool. However, under subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition of qualified expenditure in subsection 127(9), only 80% of the arm's-length contract payment is included in the qualified expenditure base for the section 127 Investment Tax Credit. Furthermore, to prevent duplicate claims on the same underlying R&D activity, if a contractor performs SR&ED in Canada on behalf of a Canadian payor, subsection 127(18) requires the contractor to reduce its own qualified expenditures by the amount of the contract payment received or receivable from the Canadian client. Conversely, if a Canadian engineering or software firm performs SR&ED under contract for a foreign client (who has no Canadian tax presence and cannot claim SR&ED), the Canadian performer is generally entitled to claim the SR&ED tax credits on its own eligible Canadian payroll and costs because no Canadian payor is entitled to a deduction under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01).

Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length (related) party, the payer receives 0% ITC on the payment under subsection 127(9). To preserve the tax credit within a corporate group where one entity owns the intellectual property and another related entity employs the R&D personnel, the parties must execute a formal Transfer of Qualified Expenditures Agreement (Form T1146) under subsections 127(13) to (20), transferring the performer's actual underlying qualified expenditures (capped at the contract amount) to the related payer.

Third-Party Payments—defined under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) as payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to the taxpayer's business and where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results—are similarly included at 100% in the section 37 pool and at 80% in section 127 qualified expenditures. Special administrative rules apply to agricultural producers making levy contributions to approved agricultural organizations that fund SR&ED: agricultural producers are exempt from completing project narratives in Form T661 for those contributions and instead report their 80%-included agricultural SR&ED contributions directly on T2 Schedule 31, Part 8, Line 350.
Overhead Elections: Prescribed Proxy Amount Versus Traditional Method

Claimants must elect on Line 160 of Part 1 of Form T661 whether to calculate SR&ED overhead using the Prescribed Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. Under section 37 of the ITA, this election must be made on the first Form T661 filed for the taxation year and is legally irrevocable for that taxation year once submitted; a taxpayer cannot amend a return to switch between the Proxy and Traditional methods after initial filing.

Under the Prescribed Proxy Method (governed by subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations), instead of identifying, tracking, and substantiating individual overhead expenses, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base. Tax auditors must strictly verify that the 55% statutory rate is applied: while the proxy rate was 65% for taxation years prior to 2013 and 60% in 2013, it has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 2014, meaning any claim or advisory document applying a 65% proxy rate in 2026 is erroneous and overstates the proxy base by 10 percentage points. The PPA is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 and flows directly into Part 4 as a qualified expenditure for the section 127 ITC, subject to the overall proxy cap under Regulation 2900(6); actual business overhead expenses (such as facility rent, utilities, and administrative support) remain deductible under section 9 of the ITA as ordinary business expenses and do not enter the section 37 SR&ED pool.

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant foregoes the 55% notional PPA and instead claims actual overhead and other expenditures in both the section 37 deduction pool and the section 127 qualified expenditure pool. To qualify under the Traditional Method, every claimed overhead item must satisfy a two-prong statutory test: it must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, and it must be strictly incremental—meaning the cost would not have been incurred by the business but for the execution of the SR&ED activities. Because the Traditional Method imposes an intensive contemporaneous accounting burden to prove incrementality on every invoice, it is predominantly utilized by capital-intensive manufacturing or laboratory operations whose incremental shop-floor utilities, specialized consumables, and non-proxy support costs exceed 55% of their direct SR&ED payroll.
Materials Consumed Versus Materials Transformed and Recapture Provisions

Direct materials claimed on Form T661 must consist of tangible physical property that is either consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed encompass tangible substances, chemical reagents, testing substrates, or components that are destroyed, evaporated, or rendered virtually valueless as a direct result of experimental trials, destructive testing, or laboratory analysis. Materials transformed encompass raw materials or sub-assemblies that are physically integrated or modified into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test rig constructed to test a scientific or technological hypothesis.

If an experimental prototype, custom machine, or batch of transformed material that previously generated an SR&ED ITC is subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial production use, subsections 127(27) to 127(35) of the ITA trigger SR&ED ITC Recapture. Under the recapture rules, the lesser of the original qualified expenditure of the property and the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value at the time of commercial conversion), multiplied by the ITC rate originally claimed on those materials, is added directly back to the taxpayer's Part I federal income tax payable in the year of sale or conversion.
Reinstatement of Capital Property and Equipment Lease Expenditures

One of the most impactful provisions of Bill C-15 is the restoration of SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures and equipment lease costs, which had been completely excluded between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024. Effective for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and for equipment lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024, taxpayers may once again include these outlays in their section 37 deduction pool (under paragraph 37(1)(b)) and their section 127 qualified expenditure pool (via subparagraph (a)(iv) of the definition of qualified expenditure in subsection 127(9) and the repeal of former paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1)).

To qualify under the restored capital regime, the property must satisfy three strict statutory criteria. First, under the "All or Substantially All" (90%+) Useful Life Test, the depreciable property must be newly acquired (used equipment is ineligible for the ITC) and intended at the time of acquisition to be used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time throughout its useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada; alternatively, under the restored Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) provisions of subparagraph (a)(iii) of qualified expenditure in subsection 127(9), first-term and second-term shared-use equipment used primarily (more than 50%) for SR&ED in Canada may qualify. Second, buildings, land, leasehold interests in buildings, goodwill, and commercial inventory are expressly excluded from SR&ED capital eligibility. Third, while qualifying current expenditures within a CCPC's or ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit receive a 100% cash refund of the 35% ITC, subsection 127.1(2) restricts the refundability of the 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures and equipment lease costs to 40%, translating to a 14% cash refund and a 21% non-refundable tax credit carryforward.

For hardware, robotics, clean-technology, and artificial intelligence companies acquiring equipment that does not meet the 90% SR&ED threshold (or is used partly for commercial operations), standard Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) deductions apply outside the SR&ED pool, including CCA Class 50 (55% declining-balance depreciation for general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and AI server hardware) and CCA Class 12 (100% write-off for application software and perpetual software licences).
Treatment of Cloud Computing, IaaS, SaaS, and Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure

A frequent compliance error in modern technology and artificial intelligence claims involves the improper inclusion of cloud computing costs—such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform (GCP) GPU cluster rentals, Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS), and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) subscriptions—as direct SR&ED materials or subcontract expenditures. Under CRA administrative policy and the statutory text of section 37 and subsection 127(9), cloud computing and SaaS subscriptions are intangible service operating expenses; they do not constitute physical tangible property and therefore cannot be claimed as "materials consumed or transformed," nor can they be capitalized into a CCA class or claimed as restored paragraph 37(1)(b) capital property. Similarly, because cloud providers merely supply automated compute capacity rather than performing systematic experimental investigation on behalf of the claimant in Canada, cloud invoices do not qualify as SR&ED contract expenditures.

Consequently, the treatment of cloud computing expenses turns entirely on the claimant's overhead election on Line 160 of Form T661. If a software or AI company elects the Prescribed Proxy Method (55% PPA), cloud computing and software licence fees are statutorily deemed to be overhead captured within the 55% notional proxy allowance and cannot be claimed separately on Form T661. Only if a claimant elects the Traditional Method can cloud computing costs potentially be claimed as overhead, and only to the extent that the claimant maintains granular telemetry proving that specific cloud instances were directly related and strictly incremental to the SR&ED experiments (excluding commercial hosting or production environments) and meet Canadian nexus requirements. In all cases, uncredited SaaS and cloud hosting costs remain 100% deductible as ordinary current operating expenses in computing business income under section 9 of the ITA.

body.text: Administrative Governance, Compliance Forms, and Filing Procedures
Governing Authorities and the Pre-Claim Approval Process

At the federal level, tax policy and statutory drafting reside with the Department of Finance Canada, while technical and financial compliance reviews are executed solely by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through its specialized SR&ED Directorate, which comprises Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) who evaluate scientific and technological eligibility, alongside Financial Reviewers who audit expenditure quantum and tax calculations. Unlike several European jurisdictions where an innovation ministry must pre-certify R&D projects before the tax authority processes the return, the federal Canadian SR&ED system integrates both technical and financial administration within the CRA.

To increase predictability and reduce post-filing audit friction for small and medium-sized enterprises, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026, pursuant to the modernization reforms of Bill C-15. This elective service is open to eligible Canadian businesses with gross business income below $25,000,000. Before filing the annual corporate income tax return—and prior to or during the execution of the R&D project—an eligible business may submit Form T1322 electronically through the CRA's My Business Account portal, providing a technical summary of the proposed SR&ED project and estimated expenditures. Once approved by the CRA, the pre-claim determination confirms the technical eligibility of the proposed SR&ED project for a period of up to three taxation years, provided the work is carried out as described. While pre-claim approval does not replace the mandatory annual filing of Form T661, when the claimant subsequently files Form T661 reporting its pre-claim approval case number and actual expenditure quantum, the claim is placed into a 90-day fast-track processing window, cutting the standard 180-day review timeline in half.
Line-by-Line Architecture of Form T661 and Schedule 31

A complete federal SR&ED claim is not a standalone application; it forms a prescribed component of the taxpayer's annual income tax return. Corporations must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) together with T2 Schedule 31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) alongside their T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. Unincorporated sole proprietors and trusts file Form T661 with Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)), while partnerships file Form T661 with the Form T5013 partnership information return, allocating the section 37 deduction and section 127 ITCs to qualifying partners under subsections 127(8) to 127(8.5), with limited partners restricted from claiming SR&ED ITCs.

The 2026 revision of Form T661 is structured into 10 distinct parts, incorporating new mandatory fields for the Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) research code, pre-claim approval case numbers, and restored capital property and equipment lease reporting lines.

Aggregates allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures across all projects, tracks foreign SR&ED wages on Lines 307 and 309 (capped at 10% of Canadian wages), reports restored post-December 15, 2024 capital property and lease costs, and computes the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (including Line 515 and prior-year pool adjustments on Lines 552/554).

Computes the Section 127 Qualified Expenditure Pool by taking eligible salaries, adding the 55% PPA from Part 5, including arm's-length Canadian contracts and third-party payments at 80%, adding eligible capital/lease costs, and subtracting government assistance, provincial tax credits, non-government assistance, and prescribed excluded expenses.

body.text: The 18-Month Statutory Filing Bar and Audit Defence Timelines

The single strictest procedural rule in Canadian R&D taxation is the 18-month statutory filing deadline codified in subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of investment tax credit in subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Under these provisions, a taxpayer must file Form T661 and Schedule 31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information for a particular expenditure on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporate claimant has exactly 18 months from the end of its fiscal year to file a complete SR&ED claim; for example, a corporation with a December 31, 2024 fiscal year-end must file its Form T661 and Schedule 31 on or before June 30, 2026.

Tax auditors and corporate controllers must observe three absolute legal realities regarding this 18-month bar. First, there is no ministerial discretion or fairness relief: the Income Tax Act contains no statutory mechanism permitting the Minister of National Revenue or the Tax Court of Canada to waive or extend the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, as the general taxpayer relief and "fairness" provisions of subsection 220(3.2) of the ITA do not apply to subsection 37(11) or paragraph 127(9)(m). Second, late-filed expenditures suffer permanent forfeiture: any project or expenditure line omitted or filed even one day after the 18-month deadline is statutorily deemed not to be an expenditure on SR&ED, resulting in permanent forfeiture of both the section 37 deduction and the section 127 ITC for that expenditure. Third, while claimants legally have 18 months to file, submitting the SR&ED claim electronically within the initial 6-month T2 on-time filing window significantly expedites processing. Under CRA service standards, a refundable claim accepted as filed without audit is targeted for processing within 60 calendar days (and within 90 calendar days under the new April 1, 2026 pre-claim approval fast-track), whereas a claim selected for technical and financial review is targeted for completion within 180 calendar days of receiving a complete claim. If the CRA issues a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment reducing or denying an SR&ED claim, the taxpayer must file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days of the date printed on the Notice of Assessment, with a statutory window to apply for an extension of time within one year after the expiration of that 90-day period.
Judicial Precedents and Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence
Foundational Jurisprudence: Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, and CW Agencies

While subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act provides the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development"—encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken in a field of science or technology by means of a systematic investigation or search through experiment or analysis to achieve scientific or technological advancement—the practical legal test applied by both the Tax Court of Canada and the CRA's administrative guidelines is anchored in the landmark jurisprudence of the federal courts.

The foundational judicial authority in Canadian SR&ED law is Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC), authored by Justice Donald Bowman (subsequently Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada). In evaluating complex physical hydraulic modelling projects, Justice Bowman established the canonical Five-Question Test that remains the binding legal standard for determining whether work constitutes SR&ED in Canada. First, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Uncertainty exists when the probability of achieving a given technical objective, or the methodology required to achieve it, cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge and experience; routine engineering—defined as the application of established techniques, standard procedures, or publicly available data by competent professionals—does not qualify, even if the engineering task is complex, expensive, or novel to the specific company. Second, the court examines whether the claimant formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, requiring a five-stage methodical progression comprising the observation of the subject matter of the problem, the identification of the specific technological uncertainty, the formulation of a testable causal hypothesis, the methodical testing of the hypothesis through experiment or analysis, and the logical evaluation of results to confirm, modify, or reject the hypothesis. Third, the court evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through a systematic, structured, and analytical investigation rather than intuitive, unguided, or random "trial-and-error". Fourth, the court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement, defined as the generation of new scientific or technological knowledge that advances the understanding of the underlying technology relative to the baseline of publicly available knowledge. Crucially, Northwest Hydraulic established that commercial success is irrelevant and that the rejection of a hypothesis—proving systematically that a plausible technological pathway fails due to newly discovered physical or systemic constraints—is itself a valid technological advancement. Fifth, the court considers whether a detailed contemporaneous record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed; although the absence of formal laboratory notebooks is not an automatic statutory bar if other verifiable contemporaneous evidence exists, a claimant bears the burden of proving through real-time records—such as experiment logs, test data, version-control commits, failure logs, and time records—that a systematic investigation actually took place.

In consolidating its administrative eligibility framework and structuring Part 2, Section B of Form T661 into Lines 242, 244, and 246, the CRA synthesized Justice Bowman's five questions into the Three-Criteria Administrative Test: (1) Scientific or Technological Uncertainty (Line 242, capturing Question 1); (2) Systematic Investigation or Search (Line 244, capturing Questions 2, 3, and 5); and (3) Scientific or Technological Advancement (Line 246, capturing Question 4).

Immediately following Northwest Hydraulic, the Federal Court of Appeal cemented these principles in two binding appellate decisions. In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal expressly approved Justice Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic criteria and addressed the evidentiary standard for repeatability and objective verification. The Court held that while credible oral testimony from technical witnesses is admissible, the core hallmark of scientific and experimental development is that the testing and results must be documented with sufficient precision to allow verification or reproduction; without objective documentary evidence of the testing data, a taxpayer cannot discharge its burden of proof. Shortly thereafter, in CW Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, [2002] 1 C.T.C. 211 (FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal held that the five Northwest Hydraulic questions are sequential and cumulative, establishing that technological uncertainty is the strict threshold condition. If a taxpayer fails to prove that a genuine technological uncertainty existed at the outset of the project—as opposed to a business, market, or routine functional design challenge—the inquiry ends and the claim fails regardless of how systematically the engineering team worked.
Contemporary Tax Court Rulings on Software, Manufacturing, and Documentation

Subsequent and recent jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) between 2006 and 2026 has refined how the Northwest Hydraulic test applies across software engineering, advanced manufacturing, energy, and food processing.

In the realm of software architecture versus routine product development, the Tax Court emphasized in Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, and subsequent software appeals that writing complex code or using modern development frameworks does not automatically constitute SR&ED unless the developer confronts an underlying algorithmic or architectural limitation that cannot be resolved using documented software engineering patterns. However, in a pivotal 2024 software decision (2024 TCC 129), the Tax Court ruled in favour of a claimant developing a cloud-based SaaS platform integrating open-source tools (React and Redux), holding that systemic uncertainty arose when integrating disparate open-source frameworks under extreme performance constraints. The court encouraged a holistic evaluation of software projects where system-level interactions create unpredictable bottlenecks beyond routine debugging or optimization, provided the claimant substantiates the investigation with quantitative performance metrics and credible developer testimony. Conversely, in the SCADACOM-5 litigation, the court upheld a $1,293,692 disallowance where the software work consisted of modernizing and scaling up a legacy system using known tools—confirming that software modernization and scale-up represent routine product development rather than experimental development.

With respect to contemporaneous documentation and public domain knowledge, the Tax Court dismissed an appeal concerning a solar shingle development project in Logix Data Products Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 36. The court identified three fatal defects in the claim: the taxpayer failed to demonstrate technological uncertainty because the required engineering knowledge already existed in the public domain; no structured experimentation was performed to achieve a technological advancement; and the taxpayer failed to maintain contemporaneous records and documents substantiating the work performed.

Recent 2025 and 2026 decisions have further reinforced the rejection of trial-and-error prototyping and retrospective wage estimation. In 2025 TCC 63, involving mobile direct-contact water heaters for hydraulic fracturing in the energy sector, the Tax Court denied the claim because the field adjustments constituted unguided trial-and-error prototyping supported only by vague, generalized post-hoc hypotheses and lacked expert or contemporaneous documentary evidence. Similarly, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2025 TCC 183, the Tax Court dismissed claims spanning 13 food-processing projects after finding no proven technological uncertainty, no systematic hypothesis testing with contemporaneous records, and a fatally flawed financial methodology in which employee wages were retrospectively estimated and split evenly across production batches rather than tracked through verifiable time records. By direct contrast, a 2025 food-science appeal involving shelf-stable cold-pressed juice ("Chrisoda") succeeded in the Tax Court because the claimant formulated specific hypotheses regarding novel High-Pressure Processing (HPP) parameters for microbial stability and tested them systematically using recorded, quantitative laboratory observations of pH levels and microbial counts. Finally, in 2026 FCA 175 (Tuna Temple), the Federal Court of Appeal re-examined the interplay between Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, and CW Agencies regarding the evidentiary weight of credible witness testimony when evaluating technological uncertainty and systematic investigation in Tax Court appeals.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Regimes

Every Canadian province and the Yukon Territory operates a dedicated R&D tax credit or grant program that stacks on top of the federal SR&ED program. With the exception of Quebec and Alberta—which administer their own distinct tax and grant filings through Revenu Québec and Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, respectively—provincial R&D tax credits harmonize with the federal definition of qualified expenditure under subsection 127(9) and are administered directly by the CRA via provincial schedules attached to the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return.
Quebec: The CRIC Overhaul and the Transition from CDAE to CDAEIA

Quebec maintains the most generous—and most recently restructured—provincial innovation tax regime in Canada, administered by Revenu Québec alongside technical and sectoral certifications issued by Investissement Québec (IQ) and the Ministry of the Economy, Innovation and Energy (Ministère de l'Économie, de l'Innovation et de l'Énergie).

In the 2025–2026 Quebec Budget (delivered March 25, 2025), the Government of Quebec enacted a sweeping consolidation of its R&D tax architecture, abolishing six separate legacy tax credits: the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly claimed on Form RD-1029.7), the Tax Credit for University Research or Public Research Centre Contracts, the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research, the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (subject to transitional relief for eligible fee balances up to December 31, 2029), the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, and the industrial design component of the In-House Design Tax Credit.

In their place, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec instituted the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation). The CRIC operates as a fully refundable tax credit for corporations with an establishment in Quebec carrying on a business there, providing an enhanced rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures in excess of the exclusion threshold (shared among an associated corporate group), and a base rate of 20% on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 tier. Crucially, the 30% enhanced CRIC rate is available to all corporations regardless of asset size or public/private ownership on the first $1,000,000 of net eligible spending. Beyond traditional SR&ED, the CRIC expands scope to include pre-commercialization activities such as regulatory homologation, certification testing, and industrial product design following R&D. Eligible expenditures incurred in Quebec encompass direct employee labour, 50% of arm's-length subcontractor contracts (alongside 80% of university or eligible public research centre contracts, for which the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy continues to issue recognition certificates), and capital equipment acquisition costs, thereby harmonizing with the federal restoration of capital property eligibility. Before the 30% and 20% CRIC rates apply, a claimant must subtract an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of individual employee exclusion thresholds across all employees engaged in eligible activities; each employee's threshold equals the basic personal amount under Quebec's personal income tax system ($18,571 in 2025), prorated strictly in proportion to the percentage of working time that employee devotes to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.

Simultaneously, Quebec overhauled its flagship IT payroll incentive, transitioning from the legacy Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE) to the Development of E-Business Tax Credit Integrating Artificial Intelligence (CDAEIA) for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025. While retaining the core corporate eligibility thresholds—a minimum of 6 full-time eligible employees, at least 75% of employee time devoted to eligible activities, at least 50% of gross revenue derived from software publishing, data processing, and hosting, and at least 75% of eligible revenue derived from third-party services or applications used exclusively outside Quebec—CDAEIA requires that the 75% employee activity threshold specifically involve artificial intelligence integration. Starting in 2026, legacy CDAE activities such as routine system maintenance and evolution, technology infrastructure maintenance, general IT support without AI integration, routine software updates and patches, and hardware configuration are strictly excluded. Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2024, the historical $83,333 eligible salary cap per employee was abolished and replaced with an exclusion threshold per employee equal to the Quebec basic personal amount ($18,571 in 2025), prorated by time spent on eligible activities.

Although the combined CDAE/CDAEIA credit rate remains 30% of eligible labour above the exclusion threshold, the credit composition shifts progressively toward the non-refundable portion through 2028 (and starting in 2026, rates are reduced by half if 50% or more of gross revenue comes from services provided to related entities for applications used exclusively outside Quebec). Specifically, in the 2025 calendar year (the final CDAE year), the 30% credit comprises a 23% refundable component and a 7% non-refundable component; in the 2026 calendar year (the first CDAEIA year), it shifts to 22% refundable and 8% non-refundable; in the 2027 calendar year, it adjusts to 21% refundable and 9% non-refundable; and for 2028 and subsequent calendar years, it stabilizes at 20% refundable and 10% non-refundable. Corporations must apply to Investissement Québec for annual corporation and employee eligibility certificates within 15 months following the end of their fiscal year—for example, by March 31, 2027, for a December 31, 2025 fiscal year-end.
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and Complementary Sectoral Credits

Ontario administers two core SR&ED-aligned corporate tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), which are harmonized with federal Form T661 definitions and claimed via T2 schedules filed with the CRA. The primary incentive for small and medium-sized corporations is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566), which provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit for qualifying CCPCs on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, generating a maximum annual refundable cash credit of $240,000. Tax auditors must ensure that outdated references to a 10% OITC rate are corrected to the current statutory 8% rate. Unlike the federal expenditure limit (which doubled to $6,000,000 under Bill C-15), Ontario's OITC expenditure limit remains capped at $3,000,000 and phases out when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Complementing the OITC is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508), which provides a 3.5% non-refundable corporate income tax credit on all eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (after deducting the OITC, which constitutes government assistance for ORDTC purposes) with no expenditure limit and no corporate size restriction. Unused ORDTC credits can be carried back 3 years and forward 20 years to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable.

In addition to OITC and ORDTC, Ontario technology and manufacturing businesses frequently stack two specialized provincial tax credits: the Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (OIDMTC), which provides a 40% refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario labour (35% for fee-for-service work) for interactive digital products, software games, and educational media with no overall dollar cap; and the Ontario Made Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit (OMMITC), enhanced in 2025 to provide up to a 15% refundable tax credit for CCPCs on eligible capital investments in manufacturing buildings and machinery in Ontario.
British Columbia, Alberta, and Rest-of-Canada Regimes

Across Western, Central, Atlantic, and Northern Canada, provincial and territorial governments provide distinct R&D tax incentives that integrate with federal SR&ED claims. In British Columbia, Part 6 of the British Columbia Income Tax Act governs the BC SR&ED Tax Credit, which is claimed on Form T666 attached to the T2 return within a strict 18-month post-year-end filing deadline. British Columbia provides a 10% refundable tax credit for qualifying CCPCs (and, under Budget 2026, eligible Canadian public corporations for tax years beginning on or after December 16, 2024) on qualified BC SR&ED expenditures up to the federal expenditure limit, now $6,000,000 (yielding a maximum $600,000 annual refundable credit), and a 10% non-refundable tax credit on expenditures above the limit or for non-CCPCs. Notably, legislative amendments enacted by July 2026 eliminated the former September 1, 2027 statutory expiry date, rendering the BC SR&ED tax credit permanent.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)—administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act—provides a refundable grant and tax payment to corporations carrying on R&D in the province. The IEG delivers an 8% base payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's "base spending amount" (calculated as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta R&D spending over the two immediately preceding taxation years), and an enhanced 20% payment on incremental eligible Alberta R&D spending exceeding that two-year base, up to an annual maximum expenditure cap of $4,000,000. The IEG phases out linearly for corporations whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada lies between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000.

In Manitoba, corporations may claim a 15% R&D Tax Credit with no expenditure limit, under which 50% of the credit (7.5% effective rate) is refundable for in-house R&D, and 100% of the credit (15% effective rate) is refundable for R&D carried out under contract with qualifying Manitoba post-secondary or research institutions. Saskatchewan offers a 10% R&D Tax Credit that is refundable on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures for CCPCs (maximum $100,000 cash refund) and non-refundable for non-CCPCs or excess expenditures up to a $10,000,000 annual cap. In Atlantic Canada, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit on eligible provincial SR&ED expenditures with no expenditure cap and no restriction on corporate size. Finally, the Yukon Territory provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in the Yukon, supplemented by an additional 5% credit on payments made to Yukon University.

body.text: Non-Dilutive Federal Grants and Government Assistance Grinding Mechanics
NRC IRAP, Clean Technology Integration, and the Strategic Response Fund

Canadian corporations frequently stack upfront, discretionary government grants and repayable contributions alongside retrospective SR&ED tax credits. However, several significant federal program restructurings occurred across the 2025–2026 fiscal cycle that directly impact corporate funding strategies. NRC IRAP (National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program) remains Canada's premier direct R&D grant program for incorporated, for-profit SMEs operating in Canada with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) employees. Delivered through a network of Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs), NRC IRAP provides non-repayable financial contributions reimbursing up to 80% of internal technical salaries (and up to 50% of Canadian subcontractor costs) for pre-approved technology innovation projects. Notably, Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC) ceased operating its standalone grant intake and was formally wound into the National Research Council; clean-technology R&D applicants now apply directly through NRC IRAP Clean Technology.

At the large-enterprise scale, the former Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) was renamed and restructured into the Strategic Response Fund. It requires a $10,000,000 minimum government contribution (implying a minimum project size of $20,000,000 or more with at least 50% non-government co-funding) and a mandatory pre-application consultation prior to submitting a Statement of Interest, operating primarily as a repayable contribution for large-scale industrial and transformative capital projects rather than an SME grant. Furthermore, the Canada Digital Adoption Program (CDAP) wound down in 2025 with no federal micro-grant replacement, while Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC) experienced a $70,000,000 annual budget reduction starting in 2025–2026. Conversely, regional development agencies expanded targeted AI commercialization support—such as FedDev Ontario's Regional AI Initiative (RAII), which provides interest-free repayable contributions of $125,000 to $5,000,000 covering up to 50% of eligible AI productization and adoption costs—and Investissement Québec's ESSOR program, which operates through March 31, 2027.
Mathematical Modelling of Federal-Provincial Credit and Grant Stacking

Under paragraph 127(11.1)(b) and subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA (as well as paragraph 37(1)(d) for the deduction pool), any government assistance or non-government assistance (as defined in subsection 127(9)) that a taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the time of filing its tax return in respect of an SR&ED expenditure must be subtracted ("ground") from both the section 37 expenditure pool and the section 127 qualified expenditure pool.

Crucially, provincial R&D tax credits (such as Ontario's OITC/ORDTC, Quebec's CRIC, BC's T666 credit, and Alberta's IEG) as well as direct federal grants (such as NRC IRAP) constitute "government assistance" for federal SR&ED purposes. However, when an upfront salary grant like NRC IRAP is combined with the Prescribed Proxy Method (55% PPA), a powerful statutory leverage effect occurs: the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount under Regulation 2900(4) is calculated on the gross eligible SR&ED salary base before deducting the NRC IRAP grant; the NRC IRAP grant is only subtracted afterward in Part 4 of Form T661 when computing net qualified expenditures.

Let S represent eligible Canadian SR&ED direct salaries, M represent eligible materials, C represent arm's-length Canadian subcontractor invoices, and G represent an NRC IRAP grant covering a fraction of salaries. Under the Prescribed Proxy Method, the pre-provincial federal qualified expenditure base Q is:
Q = S + 0.55S + M + 0.80C − G

When a provincial R&D tax credit P is also earned on the same expenditure base, the net federal qualified expenditure pool Qnet and resulting enhanced 35% federal ITC (ITCfed) are determined by subtracting P as government assistance:
Qnet = Q − P; ITCfed = 0.35 × Qnet

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics across jurisdictions for the 2026 taxation year, consider a qualifying CCPC incurring $1,000,000 in direct Canadian SR&ED salaries (S, distributed across 10 full-time engineers earning $100,000 each and devoting 100% of their time to SR&ED) and $100,000 in arm's-length Canadian subcontractor costs (C), electing the 55% Prescribed Proxy Method.

Strategic Compliance Conclusions and Audit Readiness Framework

Navigating the modernized 2026 Canadian R&D tax architecture requires aligning corporate tax planning, capital budgeting, and engineering documentation with both the statutory expansions of Bill C-15 and the stringent evidentiary standards enforced by the Canada Revenue Agency and the Tax Court of Canada. With the enhanced 35% expenditure limit doubled to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs whose balance sheets carry substantial convertible debt, venture financing, or equipment liabilities exceeding $15,000,000 in taxable capital employed in Canada should proactively evaluate and file the new three-year average gross revenue election under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) to preserve their full $2,100,000 refundable federal ITC ceiling. Similarly, newly listed domestic public companies should verify their Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) status under subsections 127(10.1) and 127(10.6) rather than defaulting to the 15% non-refundable rate. Following the restoration of paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127.1(2) capital refundability, engineering and accounting teams must also maintain asset-level usage logs proving that new laboratory instruments, testing rigs, pilot machinery, and dedicated AI hardware acquired on or after December 16, 2024, satisfy the 90%+ ("all or substantially all") SR&ED operating-time test in Canada over their expected useful life.

From an evidentiary standpoint, recent Tax Court losses—including Logix Data Products (2021 TCC 36), 2025 TCC 63, and Manning Canning Kitchens (2025 TCC 183)—demonstrate that retrospectively reconstructed narratives and evenly split or estimated batch wage allocations are routinely disallowed on audit and appeal. Claimants must institutionalize real-time capture of failed trials, quantitative experimental metrics, version-control commits and issue-tracking tickets linked specifically to technological uncertainties (distinguished from routine product modernization), and contemporaneous employee time allocation records.
